Most of what you need to learn spatial omics already exists somewhere public. The problem
is not scarcity — it is that a search returns forty links with no indication of which are
maintained, which assume you already know scanpy, and which were written for a chemistry
version that no longer ships.

This page is a filter, not an index. If you want exhaustive coverage, the curated lists
below do that better and are maintained by people closer to the tools.

## What gets listed here

- **It teaches, or it is a primary reference.** Marketing pages and press releases do not
  qualify, however informative they look.
- **Its level is stateable.** If we cannot say who it is for, it is not useful to send
  anyone to.
- **It is reachable without a login, a licence, or an institutional subscription.**
- **It was checked on the date shown.** An unchecked link is a claim we are not making.

What does not get listed: anything we have not opened; anything whose last commit predates
a major API break in the tool it teaches; and any resource we would not send a specific
person to for a specific reason.

::: {.callout-note}
**Link, never host.** Everything here points at the original. We do not mirror notebooks,
reproduce figures, or copy text — most of this material is licensed for use, not for
redistribution, and "free to read" is not permission to copy.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Verification status.** Entries with a URL were opened and confirmed on the date in the
table. Entries listed **without** a link are ones we know exist by name from the aggregator
lists but have not yet opened ourselves — they are recorded so the search is not repeated,
and they are deliberately not linked until checked. That is the same rule the lessons apply
to citations.
:::

Read one of these first; come back here for opinions about what to actually use.

## Courses and workshop material

The most useful free teaching material in this field is workshop repositories. They are
written to be taught from, so they assume less than documentation does and explain more
than a paper does. The cost is that they are snapshots — a 2022 workshop teaches a 2022 API.

| Resource | Language | For whom | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|
| [theislab/spatial_scog_workshop_2022](https://github.com/theislab/spatial_scog_workshop_2022) | Python | SCOG virtual workshop notebooks with per-session conda environments. Older, but from the group behind much of the scverse spatial stack | 2026-09-01 |
| [fhausmann/workshop_spatial](https://github.com/fhausmann/workshop_spatial) | Python | Explicitly a beginner's course on Visium: visualisation, expression patterns, clustering. Start here if you have never analysed spatial data | 2026-09-01 |
| [ashoks773/SpatialTranscriptomicsWorkflow](https://github.com/ashoks773/SpatialTranscriptomicsWorkflow) | Python | End-to-end walkthrough on a public hepatocellular carcinoma dataset, from download to annotation | 2026-09-01 |
| `drieslab/giotto_workshop_2024` | R | Giotto workshop materials. Listed in the drieslab organisation; not yet opened here | — |
| `spatial-omics-tutorials` (BIML 2025) | Python / R | Tutorials and best practices from BIML 2025. Catalogued in p-gueguen's list; not yet opened here | — |
| `MGC-BioSB-Spatial-Omics-Analysis-2025` | Python | Workshop materials. Catalogued in p-gueguen's list; not yet opened here | — |

## Tool ecosystems

Choose an ecosystem before choosing a tool. Moving between them mid-project costs more than
either tool saves, and most methods exist in only one.

**Python / scverse.** `squidpy` for spatial statistics and neighbourhood analysis;
`spatialdata` for the object model and coordinate systems (lesson 6); `bento` for
subcellular analysis; `scvi-tools` for the deep-learning family including `DestVI`.

**R / Bioconductor and beyond.** `Giotto` (also has a Python interface); `Seurat` for
spatial objects; `Voyager` on `SpatialFeatureExperiment`, from the Pachter lab, oriented
around exploratory spatial data analysis; `spacexr` for RCTD deconvolution; `nnSVG` for
spatially variable genes — notable as one of the better-calibrated options, see lesson 12;
`semla` and `SPATA2` as general toolkits.

**Visualisation and browsers.** `Vitessce` (JavaScript) for integrated exploration;
`rakaia` for in-browser interactive analysis.

**GUI tools.** `VR-Omics` offers end-to-end processing without code. Worth knowing this
category exists — a substantial part of the field does not work at a command line, and the
lessons on this site assume you do.

**Platform-specific.** `CosMx-Analysis-Scratch-Space` for CosMx SMI.

*Individual tool URLs are catalogued in the three lists above and are not duplicated here.*

## Benchmarks worth reading before you choose a method

These are the papers behind the numbers quoted in the lessons. Full entries with DOIs are in
`references.bib`.

| Topic | Finding that should change what you do | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Imaging platform benchmarking | False discovery rate differs substantially by platform, and by chemistry version within a platform | 5 |
| Xenium quality assessment | Detection efficiency 1.2–1.5× Chromium v2 — targeted platforms are not "low quality" | 5 |
| Segmentation benchmarking | Cell-type calling accuracy ranged 35–74% across methods on the same simulated tissue | 7 |
| Spatially variable gene benchmarking | Most methods produce poorly calibrated p-values; rank-based selection recommended over significance cutoffs | 12 |
| Gene-category enrichment | Over 500-fold inflation of false positives with spatially autocorrelated phenotypes | 12 |

## Public data

See @sec-data-strategy for how this site uses public datasets and why none of them are
committed to the repository. Provenance, licence and checksum for every dataset actually
used live in `data/SOURCES.md`, along with searches that found nothing — a negative result
is a finding and stops the next person repeating it.

## Contributing an entry

Open an issue or a pull request with the URL, one sentence on who it is for, and the date
you opened it. Entries without a stated audience get sent back, because "useful resource"
is not information anyone can act on.

If you find a dead link or a resource that has fallen behind an API break, that is equally
worth reporting. A resource page that rots is worse than no resource page, because it looks
maintained.
